summaries.example: Imagine a coin game. If heads comes on the first toss, you win 2 points. If it comes on the second toss, you win 4 points. On the third toss, you win 8 points, and the prize keeps doubling. Each later win is less likely, but the prize is much bigger. When we multiply each prize by its chance and add everything, the total never settles on a finite number. Still, the coin will almost certainly stop fairly early, so you will probably win only a small prize.
summaries.summary: The St. Petersburg game begins with a fair coin. The coin is tossed until heads appears. A heads on toss 1 pays 2 units, on toss 2 pays 4, on toss 3 pays 8, and so on. Each prize has a matching probability: later prizes are less likely, but they grow just as quickly. When we calculate expected value, every level adds another 1, so the total grows without reaching a finite number. This seems to say that a player should pay any ordinary amount to play once. Yet the game will almost certainly end early, and the player will usually win only a modest amount. The puzzle is not a strict logical contradiction; it is a clash between a respected decision rule and ordinary ideas about sensible payment. The entry surveys many proposed solutions. Some limit how much utility a person can have, some make extra wealth matter less, and some reduce the influence of extremely small probabilities. It also examines harder cases, including games whose results depend on how an infinite sum is arranged.
key_ideas: The game uses a fair coin and prizes that double after each extra toss.
The expected value becomes larger than every ordinary, finite amount.
Most actual plays end after only a few tosses, so the player usually receives a modest prize.
This creates a conflict between a mathematical calculation and the judgment that paying an enormous price would be unreasonable.
Philosophers have suggested different responses, such as giving extra money less importance, setting a limit on value, or giving tiny chances less weight.
summaries.why_it_matters: The puzzle asks how mathematics, probability, and good decision-making should fit together. It shows that a rule that works well for ordinary gambles may give strange advice in unusual cases. Studying the puzzle helps us ask what “rational” should mean when possibilities are extremely unlikely or when values can keep growing.

important_terms.definition: A situation that seems to give a surprising or unreasonable answer, even when the steps of the argument look correct.
A number that describes how likely something is to happen.
A way to compare choices by combining how good each result is with how likely it is.
How useful or valuable a result is for a person.

questions_to_think_about: Would you pay 10 points to play? What about 1,000 points? Why?
Should a very tiny chance of a huge prize affect a choice?
Can a calculation be correct but still fail to tell us what to do?
Is money always worth more when we get more of it?

summaries.example: Compare two games using the same fair-coin pattern. In the St. Petersburg game, the payoff after toss n is 2^n units. In a Petrograd-style version, it is 2^n+1 units every time. The second game is plainly better: whichever toss first produces heads, it gives one extra unit. Ordinary expected utility cannot distinguish them, because both expected utilities diverge. Relative Expected Utility Theory tries to compare the difference between the games outcome by outcome, giving the improved game a relative value of 1. But related cases show that even this approach has limits, especially when differences involve infinite quantities.
summaries.summary: The St. Petersburg paradox begins with a fair coin tossed until the first heads. If heads appears on toss n, the payoff is 2^n. Since the probability of that result is 1/2^n, every possible level contributes 1 to expected value, producing a series that does not have a finite total. The resulting recommendation—that any finite fee is worth paying—conflicts with the fact that the actual payoff will be finite and will usually be small. The source distinguishes this practical and theoretical conflict from a formal contradiction, so “paradox” is used in a broader sense. Historically, Cramér and Daniel Bernoulli proposed that money has decreasing marginal utility: more wealth remains desirable, but additional wealth contributes less. That handles the original monetary formulation, but the modern formulation assigns the doubling payoffs directly in utility units and thereby restores the problem. Further responses bound utility, reject or revise continuity, neglect tiny probabilities, or weight probabilities nonlinearly. Each faces objections. Relative approaches compare options rather than their separate infinite totals, but they also encounter cases involving undefined differences such as infinity minus infinity. The Pasadena game adds a different difficulty: conditional convergence makes the value depend on how an infinite series is ordered. The entry therefore raises a broad question about whether maximizing expected utility is universally appropriate.
key_ideas: The original monetary puzzle can be softened by decreasing marginal utility: additional wealth matters less as wealth rises.
The modern version places the doubling pattern directly on the agent’s utility scale, so decreasing marginal utility does not automatically solve it.
Every actual prize can be finite even though the expected utility is not finite; this involves potential, not necessarily completed, infinity.
Proposals to dismiss unrealistic banks or limited playing time do not settle the issue, because idealized versions can be constructed to avoid those practical limits.
Ignoring sufficiently small probabilities may produce finite values, but the required threshold and the reason for using it remain disputed.
The Pasadena game shows that even a conditionally convergent series can yield different results when its terms are rearranged, challenging a simple use of expected utility.
summaries.why_it_matters: Decision theory aims to explain which choices are rational, not merely to calculate averages. The St. Petersburg and Pasadena cases test whether familiar principles remain coherent when probabilities, utilities, or sums are unbounded. They also expose distinctions between actual outcomes and expectations, between practical realism and mathematical idealization, and between a theory’s formal axioms and the judgments it is meant to guide. No single solution is presented as conclusively settling every issue.

important_terms.definition: The principle that evaluates an uncertain option by multiplying each outcome’s value by its probability and adding the results.
A representation of how desirable an outcome or prospect is for a particular agent.
A pattern in which each additional unit of wealth adds value, but adds less than the previous unit.
A utility scale with an upper limit, so no outcome has value beyond some finite bound.
A condition requiring that an intermediate option be matched by some probability mixture of a worse and a better option.
A proposed decision rule that gives less influence to very small probabilities rather than treating them in the ordinary linear way.
A method that compares two acts by calculating the expected difference in their utilities, rather than assigning each act an isolated total.
An infinite series that converges, while the series formed from the absolute values of its terms does not.

questions_to_think_about: Does a rational theory need to apply to highly idealized games that could never be offered in ordinary life?
Should continuity be retained if it produces the St. Petersburg result, or rejected in such cases?
Is it rationally permitted, or rationally required, to ignore sufficiently small probabilities?
Why should one game be preferred when it improves on another in nearly every possible outcome but not all of them?
What does the Pasadena case suggest about the order in which infinite contributions should be combined?

summaries.example: Suppose a game uses a fair coin. Heads on the first toss wins 2 tickets, heads on the second wins 4, and heads on the third wins 8. The prize doubles each time, but the chance of reaching that stage is cut in half. For the first result, the calculation is 1/2 × 2 = 1. For the second it is 1/4 × 4 = 1, and the same happens again and again. Adding all those 1s gives no finite total. The strange advice would be that paying any finite number of tickets is reasonable. But most plays finish quickly, so paying millions of tickets seems foolish. The disagreement is about whether the calculation, the decision rule, or our assumptions about value need to change.
summaries.summary: In the St. Petersburg game, a fair coin is tossed until heads appears. A win on toss n pays 2^n units. The probability of that win is 1/2^n, so each possible stage contributes the same amount to expected value. Adding all the contributions produces a total larger than every finite number. The puzzle is that this seems to recommend paying any finite price, even though the game will almost certainly stop after a relatively small number of tosses. The source explains that this is not a strict contradiction in logic, but it is a serious challenge to a standard rule for rational choice. Early proposals focused on money: since extra wealth may bring smaller and smaller benefits, the expected utility can become finite. The modern version avoids that answer by placing the growing prizes directly on a person’s utility scale. Other proposals limit utility, question the continuity assumptions used in expected-utility theories, or permit small probabilities to be ignored. These proposals have their own difficulties. The entry also discusses relative comparisons between games and the Pasadena game, where an infinite alternating sum can receive different values if its terms are rearranged. The larger lesson is that expected utility may not work without qualification for every risky choice.
key_ideas: The St. Petersburg game makes every stage contribute the same positive amount to expected value, so the total is not finite.
The player will receive a finite prize in any ordinary outcome, yet the game’s expected utility can still be unbounded.
One response says that money should have decreasing marginal utility; another says utility itself should be bounded.
Practical objections about banks, time, or available money may not defeat an idealized mathematical example.
Ignoring tiny chances can avoid the puzzle, but people disagree about why this is justified and how tiny is tiny enough.
The Pasadena game shows that infinite calculations can be sensitive to ordering, creating another challenge for expected utility theory.
summaries.why_it_matters: The paradox connects probability to everyday ideas about fairness and sensible behavior. It teaches that a mathematical average is not automatically a complete decision rule, especially when there are infinitely many possible outcomes. It also shows why philosophers examine the assumptions behind a theory instead of simply accepting or rejecting its final answer.

important_terms.definition: A puzzle in which reasoning appears to lead to a conclusion that conflicts with a strong common-sense judgment, without necessarily producing a formal contradiction.
The chance that a particular event will occur.
The importance or desirability an outcome has for a particular person.
The value found by combining each possible result with its probability and adding the contributions.
The idea that gaining more money is good, but each additional amount helps less than the amount before it.
A value system that does not rise beyond some finite upper limit.
A proposed rule saying that outcomes with sufficiently tiny probabilities may be left out of a decision calculation.
A game whose infinite payoff calculation can change when the same terms are added in a different order.

questions_to_think_about: Would you trust the expected-utility calculation or your judgment about a reasonable entry price?
Does decreasing marginal utility solve the modern utility-based version of the game?
Should a decision rule be designed for imaginary cases as well as ordinary choices?
When, if ever, is it acceptable to ignore a very small probability?
Why might changing the order of addition matter when all the same outcomes are still present?
